label: q fed back as input during the copy phase
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase (t > L), on steps where the input token is q, i.e. the model is re-reading its own previously emitted q. Never fires on q in the original phase, on <DEL>, or on any other input token (2 stray tiny activations on g/3 out of 80k). Covers ~100% of activation mass; ~12% of copy-phase q inputs are inactive, mostly the earliest copy steps (q at original position 0 or 1 being fed back). Magnitude is weak at the first copy steps (recall_idx 1-2, ~0.1-0.4 of max) and largest for q fed back at later positions (recall_idx >= 3); restricting to recall_idx >= 2 raises precision to 0.93 but lowers F1 to 0.90. Not modulated by output token, next output, or L in any notable way.

issues: The claims hold up. On test, the base predicate scores P=0.879, R=1.000, F1=0.935, mass recall 1.000. The profile shows 0 activations in the original phase and 0 on <DEL>. Off-predicate activations come to 3 test steps (g and t inputs, at most 0.09 of max), holding 0.0% of the mass.

The false positives (about 11k on test) are not a new class. Precision rises with how late q is fed back: recall_idx 1 gives P=0.64, recall_idx 2 gives P=0.76, and recall_idx >= 3 gives P=0.98. About 1k inactive cases remain at recall_idx >= 3, mostly when q was original token 2. So 'mostly at the earliest copy steps' is accurate.

L does not split the recall_idx 1 false positives (P=0.650 for L<=5, P=0.651 for L>=7). prev_tok being a digit and in_count>=2 shift precision somewhat but give no clean rule. This looks like weaker firing early in the copy phase, which can't be cut cleanly.
Tightening the predicate lowers test F1 (recall_idx>=2: 0.898; recall_idx>=3: 0.823), so the simpler predicate is the right choice.
The label 'q fed back as input during the copy phase' matches the predicate and does not overclaim.
